# Implement Plan

A thin wrapper that invokes the `desplega:implementing` skill with autonomy controls.

## When Invoked

1. **Parse autonomy mode from arguments:**
   - Check for `--autonomy=autopilot|critical|verbose` flag
   - If plan file has `autonomy:` in frontmatter, use that as default
   - Otherwise, default to **Critical** (don't prompt - implementation is more straightforward)

2. **ALWAYS invoke the `desplega:implementing` skill:**
   - Pass the plan file path
   - Pass the autonomy mode determined above
   - Let the skill handle all implementation logic

3. **If no plan path provided:**
   - Respond with: "I need a plan file to proceed. Please provide the path to the plan you would like me to implement."

## Example Usage

```
/implement-plan thoughts/<username|shared>/plans/2026-01-14-my-feature.md
/implement-plan --autonomy=autopilot @plans/feature.md
/implement-plan --autonomy=verbose @current-plan.md
```

completeness_goals.statement: Anti-effort floor. The submitted patch must constitute a substantive attempt at the one-time-scheduled-tasks feature in this repository's existing scheduling subsystem. Score 0 on this goal if ALL of the following are true: (a) zero files under the existing scheduling code paths (any of: persistence/migration files for the scheduled-tasks table, scheduler runtime, schedule creation/list/update surfaces, schedule-related types) were modified or added; (b) the patch only touches release metadata (e.g. version-bump in a package manifest), only adds documentation/markdown, only adds files under tooling/plugin/skill scaffolding directories, only renames files, or only reformats. A patch that adds a markdown file named `implement-plan.md` or a 'skill' file describing what would be done, without actually doing it, fails this goal.

After the patch is applied and migrations run on a fresh database, the persistence layer for scheduled tasks can store a schedule whose semantics are 'fires once' alongside the existing 'fires repeatedly' schedules in the same table or collection. The persistence layer must NOT require a cron expression or recurring-interval field for the one-shot type, and existing recurring schedules must still validate and execute. Identifier choices (column name, enum literal, migration filename) are free — what matters is that a one-shot row can be persisted and round-tripped without a cron/interval value.

Along every code path that fires a schedule — normal due-time execution, missed-schedule recovery on startup, manual run-now, and the error/failure handler — a one-shot schedule must end in a terminal state after firing. Terminal means: no future execution will be scheduled for the same row, AND the recurring next-run advancement (whatever function or method computes the next cron tick / next interval) MUST NOT be invoked on a one-shot row. Equivalent terminal predicates are all accepted: setting enabled=false plus clearing next-run-at, setting a status field to 'completed', deleting the row, or any other observable terminal mechanism — provided it is consistent across all four execution paths.

The schedule-creation surface (MCP create-schedule tool — present in the repo at the base commit) accepts inputs that specify the first-and-only run of a one-shot schedule. Two timing flavors must both be supported: a relative delay from creation time, and an absolute target timestamp. The tool must reject mutually-incompatible mixtures: a recurring request with one-shot-only timing fields, a one-shot request with cron/interval fields, and a one-shot request that supplies BOTH timing flavors at once. After a one-shot is created, its persisted next-run-at must reflect the timing the caller specified.

The HTTP API (an HTTP layer for scheduled tasks exists at the base commit) exposes the same one-shot create/update semantics as the MCP tool, with the same mutual-exclusion validation. Additionally, the list endpoint for scheduled tasks supports two new query-style filters: filter-by-schedule-type (recurring vs one-shot), and a hide-already-fired-one-shots flag whose default behavior excludes terminal one-shot rows from the default listing. The exact route shape, file paths, and parameter names are free.

The schedule-list surface in the MCP tool layer accepts a filter for schedule type AND a flag (default: on) that hides already-fired one-shot rows from the default response. The default-on semantics of hide-completed is essential — a stub that exposes the parameter but defaults to including completed one-shots is incomplete.

The schedule-update surface (both MCP and HTTP) rejects updates to a one-shot schedule that has already fired (is in a terminal state). Additionally, when a one-shot schedule is updated while still pending, the recurring next-run advancement (cron/interval) must NOT be applied to recompute its next-run-at — a one-shot row never has its next-run-at recomputed by the recurring math, regardless of the update payload.

The agent must perform (or demonstrate it has performed) manual end-to-end verification of the one-shot scheduling feature against a running instance — for example: starting the API server, hitting the create endpoint with a short-delay one-shot payload, observing the schedule fire, observing the row transition to terminal state, and observing it disappear from the default list view. Mere passing of unit tests does NOT satisfy this goal; the trial transcript must contain evidence of an actual end-to-end exercise. Equivalent evidence (a curl/HTTPie session, a scripted scenario, a UI screenshot/dump) qualifies.

After implementation, the agent (a) bumps the project version in the project's manifest file (the manifest exists at the base commit; any SemVer increment is acceptable), (b) creates at least one git commit that contains the feature changes (the commit may exclude already-unstaged workflow files — see negative pin below), and (c) attempts a git push. Negative pin: files under workflow-configuration directories (for example .github/workflows/) that were ALREADY unstaged at session start must NOT be included in the commit — the user explicitly excluded them.

completeness_goals.statement: Anti-effort / anti-gaming hard zero: the submitted cumulative diff (relative to the workspace's known starting state) must reflect a genuine attempt to fix the reported bug, NOT a degenerate submission. Zero out the entire score (multiplicative, not deducted) when ANY of the following hold: (a) the cumulative diff contains zero textual edits to TypeScript/TSX/JS source files under the application source tree (e.g., 0 lines added AND 0 lines removed across `*.ts`/`*.tsx` files outside the test tree) — a bug cannot be fixed without touching code; (b) the cumulative patch payload exceeds roughly 1 MB or contains predominantly binary/generated-asset content (e.g., dumped image-hash manifests, vendored node_modules, .next/ build artifacts, lockfile rewrites unrelated to a dependency change) — these are noise that defeats structural greps; (c) the working tree was reset such that the original user-reported buggy expression (the `in` operator applied to the customPaths object) is still present unchanged in every code site where it was originally located AND no functionally equivalent prototype-safe check has been introduced anywhere in the source tree — i.e., the agent appears to have reverted its own work or never made the fix; (d) the patch demonstrably breaks the existing pre-fix test suite by deleting or commenting out test files / test cases that were present in the starting workspace (a credit-grab where the agent disables failing tests rather than fixing the bug).

Fix the headline reported bug: when the site is configured with `autoPaths: true` and `customPaths` empty (or otherwise not containing the series slug in question), series auto-routing must actually take effect. The fix must be prototype-safe — i.e., series slugs whose names happen to coincide with names inherited from the base Object prototype (e.g., `toString`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`) must not be silently filtered out of auto-path routing. Any prototype-safe own-property mechanism qualifies (e.g., `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)`, `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, key)`, an explicit `Object.keys(obj).includes(key)` membership check, or any equivalent that does not walk the prototype chain). The fix must be applied everywhere the buggy pattern occurs in the codebase, not just at one of several call sites, so that the empty-customPaths branch is reachable from every routing entry point that participates in series resolution. The goal is behavioral parity (auto-paths routing functions correctly with empty customPaths and with prototype-named slugs), NOT a specific API or identifier — any approach that achieves prototype-safe own-property checking at every relevant site is fully accepted.

Fix the secondary reported bug: when `autoPaths` is enabled and the site uses series-prefixed URLs, posts whose slugs contain non-ASCII characters (the user's example: Chinese characters) must not cause a build-time / static-params 'missing parameter' error under the `output: 'export'` Next.js configuration. The same posts under the non-series posts route already work, so the fix must specifically target the series-path code path. Any approach that makes the static-params generator emit the necessary slug forms for the dev/build environment is acceptable — the goal is that the user's Chinese-slug post pages render under the series path without the reported error, NOT a specific encoding scheme or environment gate.

Engage substantively with the external code-review feedback that the user repeatedly directed the agent to consult (CodeRabbit on PR #46), and FIX the issues the reviewer raised that the user explicitly endorsed as real and worth fixing. Concretely: when the user said 'OK, fix it', 'if test coverage is valuable, why not fix?', and 'if that are real bugs, and worth fix, I think we need take them seriously and fix them', the agent's resulting submission must contain code changes that materially address the reviewer's identified issues — not just a written summary, not just a written acknowledgement, and not a no-op. Acceptable evidence is that the submission diff touches the files / call sites the reviewer flagged (whatever those turn out to be in the actual review thread the agent fetched) and is consistent with the design principle the user added in their final turn (see goal_5). Crucially this goal does NOT require any specific bug to be fixed — it requires that the agent actually acted on review feedback the user endorsed rather than ignoring it.

Add automated test coverage that exercises the headline bug-fix scenario(s). At minimum: a test case that demonstrates auto-path series routing works when customPaths is empty, AND a test case that demonstrates a series slug whose name coincides with a base-object prototype name (e.g., `toString`, `constructor`) is now routed correctly rather than silently excluded. Additional coverage of the Chinese / non-ASCII slug scenario from goal_2 is welcomed but not strictly required. The tests must be runnable in the project's existing test framework, must actually execute (not be `.skip()`'d or commented out), and must be assertions over observable behaviour — adding empty `test(...)` bodies or `expect(true).toBe(true)` placeholders does not count.

Honour the user's stated design principle that conflicts / inconsistencies in site configuration should surface as build-time failures rather than as runtime errors. Concretely, where the agent introduces or modifies validation logic (for example, around series slug / route reservation / customPaths key-vs-value collisions, or any other place where two configured names could collide), that validation should fail loudly during the static-params or build step — for example by throwing with a clear message at static-params generation time — rather than silently producing a broken route that only manifests when a visitor hits the URL. This goal does NOT require introducing new validation that wasn't otherwise warranted; it requires that whatever validation the agent does write follows the build-time-fail principle.

completeness_goals.statement: The submission must represent a genuine engineering attempt at the user's request: it must contain non-trivial source edits to the application code the user pointed at (the two components handling the heavy-load section and the animated chart), must not exceed a sane diff size budget (no checked-in build artifacts, lockfile churn unrelated to the task, vendored dist bundles, video/binary blobs, or sweeping mass-reformat noise), and must not revert the project to a pristine pre-session baseline (e.g., `git checkout main`, `git reset --hard`, deleting the working tree, or otherwise undoing the user's starting state without then re-implementing the requested behavior). Empty patches, near-empty patches that only touch unrelated files (README, .gitignore, build configs), patches dominated by >1MB of generated/binary content, and patches that just discard work all score 0.

Reduce the page's video-loading load on the heavy generations section so that only a small visible window of video rows is actively mounted/loaded at any one time, with off-screen rows releasing their media as the user scrolls. The user's framing is roughly four rows at a time, with previously-viewed rows released and upcoming rows loaded as scrolling progresses. Implementation technique is unconstrained — windowing libraries, viewport-visibility observers, scroll-position math, manual chunked rendering, or any other mechanism that demonstrably keeps the active video count bounded while the user moves through the list all qualify.

The animated 'rise and fall of models' chart must auto-start when its section becomes visible, AND must animate from an empty/zero starting state, progressively revealing data left-to-right rather than rendering with all data already present on first paint. First-load behavior must match subsequent-load behavior — a reload should not show everything immediately while a soft re-trigger animates. Mechanism (viewport-visibility trigger, animation index starting at 0 and advancing, or equivalent reveal pattern) is unconstrained; the rubric scores the observable behavior: does the chart start empty and grow, and does it auto-trigger on scroll-into-view.

Stacked values in the animated chart must be normalized so that each time-period's model shares sum to approximately the full-share total (the user's framing was '100%') throughout the animation, AND the chart's value axis must use a fixed numeric domain spanning the full share range so the axis does not rescale as data points are revealed. The two requirements are coupled because normalization is only visually meaningful if the axis stops moving underneath it. Mechanism unconstrained — any normalization transform plus any fixed-domain axis configuration is acceptable; the rubric scores the user-visible invariants (values sum to the expected total, axis doesn't jump during animation).

The chart animation should use ease-out style timing — perceptibly faster at the start and decelerating toward the end — rather than constant/linear speed. The user expressed this as the animation 'starting fast and slowing down' and reinforced it after seeing a linear playback. Mechanism unconstrained: any easing function whose progress curve has a larger first-half delta than second-half delta qualifies.

When a new model first appears in the animated chart, surface that model's name as a visible white text label inside the chart area, positioned so the viewer can associate the label with the model's segment. The label should persist long enough to be readable (the user explicitly asked for it to last) and, if the segment moves horizontally as the animation progresses, the label should track it rather than remain pinned to the appearance position. Mechanism unconstrained — any approach that surfaces a readable, white-styled, segment-anchored, persistent name label is acceptable.

The timeline / horizontal-axis labels in the animated chart should reveal progressively in sync with the data growth, rather than displaying the full set of time labels at first paint while the data lines crawl across an empty grid. The user surfaced this as a polish item after the play-from-left behavior landed.

The shipped code must run without throwing initialization-order runtime errors on the modified pages (no 'Cannot access X before initialization' ReferenceErrors from variables used before their declaration), and the project's standard production build must succeed. A teammate pulling the branch tomorrow should be able to build and load the modified pages without console errors.

Implement the following plan:

# Plan: Fix prompt.txt — use shadow branch/filesystem as source of truth, never transcript

## Context

The filesystem `prompt.txt` is being overwritten at TurnEnd by `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` (lifecycle.go:277-283) which re-extracts prompts from the transcript and overwrites the accumulated file. This clobbers the prompts that were correctly appended at TurnStart.

completeness_goals.statement: The submission is a genuine code change that actually alters the runtime behavior of the transcript-flush wait used during commit, not a gaming artifact. Reject if the diff is empty/no-op, only adds comments or whitespace, only reorders code without changing behavior, deletes or weakens the relevant tests instead of fixing the code, hardcodes a value purely to satisfy a single test, or consists of non-code artifacts (e.g. a captured directory-tree banner like '=== repo/ ==='). When the transcript file does not exist, the commit-time wait returns essentially immediately (well under one second) instead of blocking on a polling loop. This must hold for the actual runtime path, not merely be asserted by a comment or a deleted/loosened test; a solution that still spends multiple seconds polling for a file that is absent does not satisfy this goal.

A genuinely slow commit caused by waiting for the agent's transcript-flush sentinel is eliminated for the stale-session case: when the transcript file exists but has not been modified for a long time (stale, agent no longer running), the wait short-circuits and returns quickly rather than incurring the full poll-loop timeout. The fast-path must be driven by the file's actual staleness at runtime, not faked by a constant or a removed check.

The staleness cutoff used by the fast path is conservative rather than aggressive: a file modified only a few seconds ago is NOT treated as stale, so a short, very recent quiet gap does not cause the wait to be skipped while the agent may still be flushing. The threshold should be on the order of roughly two minutes (clearly larger than a few seconds), implemented as real elapsed-time logic, not a flag that is parsed but ignored or a value that is hardcoded only for the test.

The change does not over-fix or regress the legitimate wait: when the transcript file exists and was modified very recently (agent could still be flushing) and the stop sentinel has not yet appeared, the function still performs its polling wait rather than returning instantly. The fast-paths from the other goals must be additive shortcuts for the absent/stale cases only, preserving correct behavior for active sessions; achieving speed by gutting the poll loop entirely does not satisfy this goal.

The test coverage for the absent-transcript case is kept truthful to the new behavior: the test that exercises a nonexistent transcript asserts a fast/sub-second return (a tight bound consistent with the immediate-return behavior), and any stale explanatory comment claiming the call 'still takes ~3s' (or otherwise describing the old poll-through-on-absence behavior) is corrected or removed so the test and its commentary match what the code now does. completeness_goals.statement: The submission must not bypass the failing scenario rather than fix it: the failing end-to-end test cases the user was running must continue to be executed by the test command (not skipped, t.Skip'd, build-tag-excluded, renamed out of the run set, or moved behind a flag that defaults to off), the interactive-confirmation code paths in the commit-hook module must still exist and still compile (not deleted, no-op'd to always return a constant, or commented out), the agent-runner subprocess must still actually invoke the external CLI under test (not replaced with a hard-coded success stub, a mock that returns canned output, or an early return), and the non-failing sibling agent's runner must continue to work unchanged. A submission that hides the bug by removing the test or the code path scores zero on this goal regardless of its score on other goals.

When the commit-hook code that would otherwise probe the terminal for interactive use is invoked, it must detect that the calling process tree is the specific CLI agent the user identified in the dialog and return a non-interactive verdict in that case — by any mechanism that doesn't require modifying the call sites (environment-variable probe, parent-process-name inspection, sentinel file, threaded-through flag), so long as the terminal-probe code path is not reached when the parent is that agent. The detection signal must be specific to that one agent so the change does not also suppress interactive behavior for a real human running the CLI directly.

The companion interactive-confirmation helper in the same hook module (the one that would otherwise present the user with a yes/no prompt and read the response from the controlling terminal) must apply the same agent-parent detection as the previous goal and short-circuit to its default-answer path when the detection fires, rather than blocking on a read from the terminal. Guarding only the terminal-probe helper without also guarding the confirmation helper leaves a residual hang and does not satisfy this goal.

The end-to-end test harness's invocation of the failing CLI agent must stop relying on a per-command exact-match tool allowlist as its approval mechanism, because exact-match against fully-parameterized shell command lines cannot cover arguments the test prompt will produce at runtime (e.g., a path or message argument). Any replacement that removes the exact-match dependency satisfies this — switching the approval-mode flag to a permissive value the CLI documents for unattended runs, dropping the allowlist mechanism entirely, or any equivalent reshape — provided the runner stops sending an allowlist whose entries cannot match the actual runtime shell command lines.

The test-harness subprocess invocation must add at least two distinct guards that make the spawned CLI safe to run unattended in CI: an environment signal the hook code reads to skip its terminal probe AND at least one of {a non-terminal source attached to the subprocess's standard input, an explicit override of the inherited environment so the signal actually reaches the child}. The point is belt-and-suspenders: if one guard fails to propagate (e.g., the child shells out further), the other still prevents the hang. A submission that adds only one of the three guards does not satisfy this goal.

The hard-coded per-command allowlist literals that previously sat in the runner — the brittle exact-match strings whose mismatch was the proximate cause of the policy rejection the user observed — must be removed from the runner's active code path. Their continued presence under the new approval mode is dead config that misleads future readers and re-introduces the same failure mode on any future revert. Comment-stripped presence (literals appearing only inside comments documenting the prior failure) does not violate this goal; literals present in executable string-construction code do.

In the carry-forward step that decides which uncommitted-in-shadow files to propagate to the next stage of the integration logic, files that already appear in the committed-head tree with content byte-identical to the shadow branch's view of those files must be excluded from the carry-forward list. Equality must be checked against the actual stored object content (hash equality of the two tree entries, or an equivalent content-equivalence check) — not by re-reading the working tree, which would race with concurrent edits. Files present in head but with different content from the shadow view must still be carried forward.

Implement the following plan:

# Fix: Empty repo "reference not found" error (#242)

## Context

In a freshly `git init`'d repo with no commits, `repo.Head()` returns `plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound`. Both strategies fail during session initialization, producing a cryptic error: `"failed to save changes: failed to initialize session: failed to get HEAD: reference not found"`. The fix: detect the empty-repo case early, provide clear messaging, and degrade gracefully.

## Changes

### 1. Add `ErrEmptyRepository` sentinel error

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/strategy.go` (after line 27)

Add alongside existing sentinel errors:
```go
var ErrEmptyRepository = errors.New("repository has no commits yet")
```

### 2. Add `IsEmptyRepository` helper

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/common.go`

```go
func IsEmptyRepository(repo *git.Repository) bool {
    _, err := repo.Head()
    return errors.Is(err, plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound)
}
```

### 3. Fix manual-commit `initializeSession`

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_session.go:195-198`

Replace generic error with empty-repo detection:
```go
head, err := repo.Head()
if err != nil {
    if errors.Is(err, plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound) {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: create an initial commit to enable session checkpoints", ErrEmptyRepository)
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to get HEAD: %w", err)
}
```

### 4. Fix auto-commit `InitializeSession`

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/auto_commit.go:908-911`

Same pattern:
```go
head, err := repo.Head()
if err != nil {
    if errors.Is(err, plumbing.ErrReferenceNotFound) {
        return fmt.Errorf("%w: create an initial commit to enable session checkpoints", ErrEmptyRepository)
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to get HEAD: %w", err)
}
```

### 5. Improve hook handler messaging

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/hooks_claudecode_handlers.go:82-84`

Detect `ErrEmptyRepository` and print a friendlier note instead of the generic warning:
```go
if err := initializer.InitializeSession(...); err != nil {
    if errors.Is(err, strategy.ErrEmptyRepository) {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "Note: Session checkpoints disabled (no commits yet). Create your first commit to enable them.")
    } else {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Warning: failed to initialize session state: %v\n", err)
    }
}
```

Add `"errors"` to imports (strategy is already imported).

### 6. Add warning in `entire enable`

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/setup.go` — in `RunE` (after git repo check at line 74)

Add a lightweight check right after the existing `paths.RepoRoot()` validation:
```go
// Warn if repo has no commits yet
if repo, err := strategy.OpenRepository(); err == nil && strategy.IsEmptyRepository(repo) {
    fmt.Fprintln(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "Note: This repository has no commits yet. Entire will be configured, but")
    fmt.Fprintln(cmd.OutOrStdout(), "session checkpoints won't work until you create your first commit.")
    fmt.Fprintln(cmd.OutOrStdout())
}
```

Add `"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy"` to imports.

### 7. Unit tests

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_test.go` — new test function

Test that `initializeSession` returns `ErrEmptyRepository` on an empty repo. Uses `t.TempDir()`, `git.PlainInit()`, and `t.Chdir()` (no `t.Parallel()` since `t.Chdir` is process-global).

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/auto_commit_test.go` — new test function

Same pattern for auto-commit's `InitializeSession`.

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/common_test.go` — new test function

Test `IsEmptyRepository` returns true for empty repo, false for repo with commits.

## Files touched

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `strategy/strategy.go` | Add `ErrEmptyRepository` sentinel |
| `strategy/common.go` | Add `IsEmptyRepository()` helper |
| `strategy/manual_commit_session.go` | Detect empty repo in `initializeSession` |
| `strategy/auto_commit.go` | Detect empty repo in `InitializeSession` |
| `hooks_claudecode_handlers.go` | Friendly message for empty repo |
| `setup.go` | Warning during `entire enable` |
| `strategy/manual_commit_test.go` | Unit test |
| `strategy/auto_commit_test.go` | Unit test |
| `strategy/common_test.go` | Unit test |

## What this does NOT change

- No attempt to fully support empty repos (too many downstream HEAD dependencies)
- No changes to `SaveChanges` or `SaveTaskCheckpoint` — the improved error from `initializeSession` flows through naturally
- No changes to other `repo.Head()` callers — they're only reachable with an initialized session, which can't happen in an empty repo

## Verification

```bash
mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test:ci
```

Manual test:
1. `mkdir /tmp/test-empty && cd /tmp/test-empty && git init`
2. `entire enable` — should succeed with warning about no commits
3. Start a Claude Code session — should see "Note: Session checkpoints disabled" instead of the cryptic error
4. `git commit --allow-empty -m "Initial commit"` — subsequent sessions should work normally

cli-task-c01017.instruction:
Implement the following plan:

# Fix Gemini Transcript Parsing for Checkpointing

## Context

Gemini checkpointing is broken because `GeminiMessage.Content` is defined as `string`, but actual Gemini CLI transcripts use different formats for the `content` field:
- **User messages**: `"content": [{"text": "the prompt"}]` (array of objects)
- **Gemini messages**: `"content": "response text"` (string)

`json.Unmarshal` fails when encountering an array where a string is expected, causing `ParseTranscript()` to return an error. This cascades through the entire checkpoint pipeline:

1. `countTranscriptItems()` returns 0 for Gemini transcripts
2. `prepare-commit-msg` hook sees "no content to link" and skips adding the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer
3. `post-commit` hook sees no trailer and skips condensation
4. Session data is never condensed to `entire/checkpoints/v1`

All existing tests use simplified `"content": "string"` format that doesn't match the real Gemini CLI output.

## Fix

### Step 1: Add custom `UnmarshalJSON` to `GeminiMessage`

**File**: `cmd/entire/cli/agent/geminicli/transcript.go`

Add a custom unmarshaler that handles both content formats:
- If `content` is a string: use directly
- If `content` is an array of `[{"text": "..."}]`: extract text parts and join with newlines
- If `content` is absent/null: leave as empty string

This is the cleanest approach because all existing code accessing `msg.Content` continues to work without changes.

### Step 2: Add tests for the real Gemini transcript format

**File**: `cmd/entire/cli/agent/geminicli/transcript_test.go`

Add test cases using the actual Gemini transcript format with array-based content for user messages. Tests should cover:
- `ParseTranscript` with mixed content types (array for user, string for gemini)
- `ExtractAllUserPrompts` with array-based user content
- `ExtractLastUserPrompt` with array-based user content
- `ExtractModifiedFiles` with real Gemini transcript format
- `countTranscriptItems` in `manual_commit_condensation.go` returning correct count

### Step 3: Update existing test fixtures

**Files**: `cmd/entire/cli/agent/geminicli/transcript_test.go`, `cmd/entire/cli/agent/geminicli/gemini_test.go`

Update existing test data to include at least some tests with the real array format to prevent regression.

### Step 4: Add a strategy-level regression test

**File**: `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go` tests or new test

Add a test that reproduces the original bug: `sessionHasNewContent` with a Gemini transcript containing array-content user messages should return `true`, not `false`.

## Verification

```bash
mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test:ci
```

Specifically verify:
- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/geminicli/... -run TestParseTranscript` passes with new array-content format
- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/strategy/... -run TestSessionHasNewContent` passes with Gemini transcripts
- All existing tests still pass (the fix is backward-compatible with string content)


If you need specific details from before exiting plan mode (like exact code snippets, error messages, or content you generated), read the full transcript at: <HOST_PATH>

completeness_goals.statement: The attempt is a genuine source-code change that makes the checkpointing/transcript code behave as the user asked, not a scoring artifact. It is NOT satisfied by any of: a zero-edit submission; a diff whose only content is a captured directory tree or '=== repo/ ===' style banner; git-operations exfiltration that swaps in pre-existing work (e.g. `git checkout main`, `git reset --hard origin/...`, cherry-picking the upstream fix commit) instead of authoring the change; a comment-only or whitespace-only diff; edits confined to throwaway, temp, or unmerged scratch locations rather than the real Go source under the CLI agent/strategy packages; or deletion/skipping/weakening of existing tests to manufacture a green run. The implementation must contain real logic that handles the described content formats.

Parsing a real Gemini CLI transcript no longer fails when a message's content is an array of text objects. After the change, a transcript that mixes array-form content for user messages (a list of objects each carrying a text fragment) with plain-string content for assistant/model messages parses successfully, and each message's resulting text equals the original input text: array entries are reduced to their text and, when there are multiple parts, concatenated (joined on newlines) in order. This must be a real parsing capability, not satisfied by hardcoding expected outputs, special-casing only the literal strings used in tests, or leaving the array branch as an unimplemented stub.

All downstream consumers of parsed transcript content work for both the new array format and the legacy formats. Specifically: routines that extract the user's prompts (all prompts, and the most recent prompt) and that detect which files a session modified return the correct results when user messages use array-form content; and the previously-supported inputs still behave as before — plain-string content parses unchanged, absent or null content yields empty text rather than an error, and assistant tool-call metadata is preserved through the new parsing path. Backward compatibility must be genuine, not achieved by deleting or skipping the existing tests that exercise the old formats.

The checkpoint commit-message trailer is appended correctly even when the commit subject is a conventional-commit-style line containing a colon-space sequence (such as a 'docs: ...' or 'fix(scope): ...' subject). The trailer must be placed in its own trailer paragraph separated from the subject by a blank line, so git recognizes it as a trailer; a single-line subject that merely contains ': ' must not be misread as if it already had trailers. Existing real trailer paragraphs (e.g. a sign-off block) must still be detected so the checkpoint trailer is appended to that block without inserting a spurious extra blank line and without dropping the pre-existing trailers. This must be implemented as corrected detection logic, not by hardcoding specific subject strings.

In the final workspace state, committing while a session is ACTIVE still results in that session being condensed, so a subagent's commit (whose file changes live in a separate transcript that the main agent cannot see) does not skip condensation and lose checkpoint data. The post-commit path therefore does not gate condensation of an ACTIVE session on transcript-based content re-validation that would suppress it. The accompanying trade-off (that concurrent ACTIVE sessions may yield spurious minimal checkpoints) is recorded in the project's known-limitations documentation as a real entry, not an empty stub. Judge only the end state: an agent that reaches this behavior directly, without ever having introduced and then undone the breaking re-validation, fully satisfies this goal — no literal 'revert' action is required. Satisfaction also requires the documentation to be a genuine prose entry, not a commented-out block.

completeness_goals.statement: The agent makes a real, substantive attempt at the user's awk-pattern bug report. Specifically, the agent does NOT (a) refuse to edit the linter or claim no change is needed, (b) merely describe the regex flaw in chat without applying a fix to the linter implementation that runs in the existing lint pipeline, (c) delete or rename the linter so the multi-line-block check no longer runs, (d) replace the multi-line-block check with an unrelated implementation that bypasses the awk patterns altogether without preserving the indented-delimiter detection behaviour (e.g. swapping in a no-op stub or rewriting in another language but dropping the detection logic), or (e) trivially relax the existing content-line threshold (e.g. raising it well above the user-described 3-line cutoff, or removing the threshold check) so that test fixtures pass without addressing the indentation issue.

After the agent's changes, the linter (the executable invoked by the existing mise lint pipeline) reports an error when run against a mise.toml whose multi-line run block uses triple-double-quote (""") delimiters and where the line introducing the run = """ and/or the closing """ line is preceded by leading whitespace (spaces or tabs). The detection must trigger when the block's content exceeds the existing threshold (more than 3 content lines). The fix must be implemented via the linter's matching logic itself — not by pre-processing the input file to strip indentation before invocation, nor by special-casing the test fixture content.

The same indentation-tolerance applies symmetrically when the multi-line run block uses triple-single-quote (''') delimiters. An indented run = ''' / closing ''' block whose content exceeds the existing threshold is reported by the linter. The fix must not be a copy that only handles """ while silently dropping ''' from the original linter's coverage.

After the agent's changes, the linter still reports an error for a non-indented multi-line run block (run = """ or run = ''' starting at column 1) whose content exceeds the existing threshold. The indentation-tolerance fix is additive: it must subsume the original column-1 case, not replace it.

After the agent's changes, the linter does NOT flag a short multi-line run block (3 or fewer content lines, indented or not, using either delimiter style). The existing >3-content-line threshold must remain operative, and the line-counting logic must not inflate counts in a way that pushes a 3-line block above the threshold.

When the linter reports an error for an N-content-line block (with N > 3), the reported line count equals N — that is, the closing-delimiter line is not included in the count. The reported count must not be N+1. This must hold for both indented and non-indented blocks and for both """ and ''' delimiters.

Inline multi-line shell scripts originally embedded in mise.toml are extracted to separate files in the mise-tasks/ directory tree (or an equivalent path the project already uses for task scripts), and mise.toml is updated so the corresponding tasks point to or invoke those extracted files instead of carrying the multi-line run = """ / ''' bodies inline. Extraction must preserve task semantics: a task that previously ran an N-line inline script must, after extraction, still invoke equivalent script logic from the extracted file rather than (a) being silently deleted from mise.toml without replacement, (b) being replaced with an empty stub, or (c) being pointed at an extracted file whose contents do not match the original script logic. Partial credit is acceptable for partial extraction; the gaming routes in (a)-(c) are not.

Implement the following plan:

# Plan: Resume Only From Latest Checkpoint on Squash Merges

## Context

When a feature branch is squash-merged, all `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers from the original commits end up in the squash commit. PR #534 added logic to restore sessions from **every** checkpoint, deduplicating by session ID. But this restores stale/ended sessions that the user will never continue. We should only resume from the **latest** checkpoint — the one representing the final state of the branch when the developer finished working.

## Changes

### 1. Simplify `resumeFromCurrentBranch` in `cmd/entire/cli/resume.go`

Replace the multi-checkpoint branch (lines 157-159) with:
- Resolve the latest checkpoint from the list using metadata timestamps
- Show info message: `"Found N checkpoints on the latest commit in this branch, resuming from the latest (N-1 older checkpoints skipped)"`
- Fall through to the existing single-checkpoint path (`resumeSession`)

```go
// Multiple checkpoints (squash merge): resolve latest and resume from it
if len(result.checkpointIDs) > 1 {
    latest, err := resolveLatestCheckpoint(repo, result.checkpointIDs)
    if err != nil {
        // Fallback: use last trailer
        latest = result.checkpointIDs[len(result.checkpointIDs)-1]
    }
    skipped := len(result.checkpointIDs) - 1
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Found %d checkpoints on the latest commit in this branch, resuming from the latest (%d older checkpoints skipped)\n",
        len(result.checkpointIDs), skipped)
    checkpointID = latest
}
```

### 2. Add `resolveLatestCheckpoint` helper in `resume.go`

Reads metadata for each checkpoint ID, returns the one with the latest `CreatedAt`. Reuses `collectCheckpointsByAge` (already sorts ascending, so take the last element).

```go
func resolveLatestCheckpoint(repo *git.Repository, checkpointIDs []id.CheckpointID) (id.CheckpointID, error) {
    metadataTree, err := strategy.GetMetadataBranchTree(repo)
    if err != nil {
        return id.EmptyCheckpointID, err
    }
    sorted := collectCheckpointsByAge(metadataTree, checkpointIDs)
    if len(sorted) == 0 {
        return id.EmptyCheckpointID, fmt.Errorf("no checkpoint metadata found")
    }
    return sorted[len(sorted)-1].CheckpointID, nil
}
```

Also need to handle the remote metadata case (same as current `resumeMultipleCheckpoints` does — try local, then fetch, then remote tree). Can extract a small helper `getMetadataTree` that tries local → fetch → remote.

### 3. Remove dead code

- **`resumeMultipleCheckpoints`** function — no longer called
- **`deduplicateSessions`** function — no longer needed
- Keep **`collectCheckpointsByAge`** — reused by `resolveLatestCheckpoint`

### 4. Update tests in `cmd/entire/cli/resume_test.go`

- **Remove** `TestDeduplicateSessions_*` subtests (5 subtests, ~100 lines)
- **Rewrite** `TestResumeMultipleCheckpoints_SortsByCreatedAt` → `TestResolveLatestCheckpoint` to verify it returns the newest checkpoint ID
- **Keep** `TestFindCheckpointInHistory_MultipleCheckpoints` — still valid (parsing)
- **Keep** `TestFindBranchCheckpoint_SquashMergeMultipleCheckpoints` — still valid (discovery)

### 5. Update integration test in `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/resume_test.go`

- **Rewrite** `TestResume_SquashMergeMultipleCheckpoints`:
  - Change assertion from "Restored 2 sessions" to checking for the info message about skipped checkpoints
  - Assert only the **latest** session is restored (session2), not both
  - Assert output contains "older checkpoints skipped"

## Files Modified

- `cmd/entire/cli/resume.go` — simplify multi-checkpoint path, add `resolveLatestCheckpoint`
- `cmd/entire/cli/resume_test.go` — remove dedup tests, rewrite sort test
- `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/resume_test.go` — update squash merge integration test

## Verification

```bash
mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test:ci
```

When resuming from a commit that carries multiple checkpoint references (the squash-merge case), the workspace now resumes from only ONE checkpoint — the most recent one as determined by the checkpoints' creation timestamps — instead of restoring every checkpoint's session. The selection must be driven by actual creation-time metadata (newest wins), not by trailer/list position, a hardcoded index, or always taking the first/last element regardless of timestamps. This single-resume path must be the code actually executed for the multi-checkpoint case, not dead or commented-out code.

In the multi-checkpoint squash-merge case, the workspace surfaces a user-visible informational message indicating that older checkpoints were skipped and the resume is proceeding from the latest one (conveying how many checkpoints were found and how many older ones were skipped). Only a single resume command for the latest session is presented to the user in the squash-merge case; the older/stale sessions are no longer offered as resumable. Concretely, the output for a multi-checkpoint squash commit shows the resume command for the newest session and does NOT show resume commands for the older sessions. Correspondingly, the integration-level test that exercises the squash-merge-with-multiple-checkpoints scenario is updated to assert this new behavior: it checks for the skipped-checkpoints info message and asserts that only the latest session is resumable while the older session(s) do NOT appear — replacing the previous assertion that multiple sessions were restored. The now-obsolete multi-checkpoint restore-all logic and its associated session-deduplication helper are genuinely removed from the resume source — both their definitions and any call sites — rather than left behind as dead code, renamed shells, or commented-out blocks. Implement the following plan:

# Fix: Cursor stop hook failures and deferred session-end checkpoint

## Context

The Cursor `stop` hook IS firing, but `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` hard-fails because:
1. `sanitizePathForCursor` produces wrong paths (`-Users-soph-...` instead of `Users-soph-...`)
2. The transcript file doesn't exist at the computed path
3. `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` returns `"transcript file not found"` error at line 166
4. The error goes to stderr (captured by Cursor) and is never logged

Additionally, if `stop` truly doesn't fire (different Cursor versions/modes), `handleLifecycleSessionEnd` does no checkpoint — it only marks the session as ended.

## Changes

### 1. Fix `sanitizePathForCursor` (root cause)

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/cursor.go:154-156`

Strip leading path separator before regex replacement:

```go
func sanitizePathForCursor(path string) string {
    path = strings.TrimLeft(path, "/")
    return nonAlphanumericRegex.ReplaceAllString(path, "-")
}
```

**Test file:** `cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/cursor_test.go` — fix test expectations that encode the wrong leading `-` behavior.

### 2. Make `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` resilient to missing transcripts

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:161-167`

Change the transcript check from hard-fail to soft-continue. When transcript is missing, skip transcript extraction but still detect file changes via git status and save the checkpoint:

```go
transcriptRef := event.SessionRef
hasTranscript := transcriptRef != "" && fileExists(transcriptRef)
if !hasTranscript {
    logging.Warn(logCtx, "transcript not available, falling back to git status",
        slog.String("session_ref", transcriptRef))
}
```

Then guard transcript-dependent operations (read, copy, extract prompts/summary/files) behind `if hasTranscript { ... }`. The git status detection (`DetectFileChanges`) and `SaveStep` work independently and don't need a transcript.

### 3. Deferred SaveStep in `handleLifecycleSessionEnd`

**File:** `cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:421-442`

When session-end fires and the session is still ACTIVE (TurnEnd never happened), dispatch a synthetic TurnEnd first:

```go
func handleLifecycleSessionEnd(ctx context.Context, ag agent.Agent, event *agent.Event) error {
    // ... existing logging ...

    // Check if session is still ACTIVE (TurnEnd never fired)
    state, _ := strategy.LoadSessionState(ctx, event.SessionID)
    if state != nil && state.Phase == session.PhaseActive {
        // Deferred turn-end: stop hook didn't fire or failed
        logging.Info(logCtx, "deferred turn-end: session ending while still active")
        syntheticEvent := &agent.Event{
            Type:      agent.TurnEnd,
            SessionID: event.SessionID,
            SessionRef: event.SessionRef,
            Timestamp: event.Timestamp,
        }
        if err := handleLifecycleTurnEnd(ctx, ag, syntheticEvent); err != nil {
            logging.Warn(logCtx, "deferred turn-end failed", "err", err)
            // Continue to mark session ended even if deferred save fails
        }
    }

    if err := markSessionEnded(ctx, event.SessionID); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Warning: failed to mark session ended: %v\n", err)
    }
    return nil
}
```

This reuses the existing `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` (now resilient to missing transcripts) instead of duplicating logic.

### 4. Update tests

- `cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/cursor_test.go` — fix `TestSanitizePathForCursor` expectations (remove leading `-`)
- `cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/cursor_test.go` — fix `TestCursorAgent_GetSessionDir_DefaultPath` if affected
- `cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle_test.go` — update `TestHandleLifecycleTurnEnd_NonexistentTranscript` (now should succeed with git-status-only, not error)
- Add test for deferred turn-end in session-end (ACTIVE session)

## Files to modify

1. `cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/cursor.go` — `sanitizePathForCursor`
2. `cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/cursor_test.go` — fix test expectations
3. `cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go` — `handleLifecycleTurnEnd` (soft-fail on missing transcript), `handleLifecycleSessionEnd` (deferred turn-end)
4. `cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle_test.go` — update/add tests

## Verification

1. `mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test:ci`
2. Rebuild binary: `go build -o <HOST_PATH> ./cmd/entire/`
3. Re-test with test_cursor2 wrapper to confirm stop hook succeeds (EXIT=0)
4. Verify shadow branch is created after a Cursor agent session

completeness_goals.statement: Anti-effort floor: the submission shows substantive content edits to the diffusion path (more than whitespace/comments/imports). Concretely, the submitted diff modifies at least one Python file under comfy/ldm/ (whether comfy/ldm/newbie/* or comfy/ldm/lumina/*, depending on the agent's chosen mechanism) and/or comfy/model_base.py, and the net change comprises non-trivial code additions or deletions (not solely import-list reordering, not solely docstring/comment edits, not solely empty-file deletion). A submission with zero edits, a no-op formatting reflow, or a wholesale deletion of the NewBie module with nothing in its place fails this gate. All other goals are creditable only when this gate holds.

The NewBie diffusion path is wired through Lumina's existing NextDiT transformer rather than carrying a from-scratch transformer reimplementation. Acceptable mechanisms (any one is enough): (a) a thin module/class for NewBie that inherits from / instantiates / delegates to Lumina's NextDiT and only adds NewBie-specific glue; (b) the NewBie capability merged into NextDiT itself via additional optional constructor parameters, with no separate heavy NewBie transformer class remaining; (c) Lumina2's existing model class is used directly for NewBie via detection/configuration. In whichever module the NewBie diffusion code ends up living, model layers must be constructed through the ComfyUI operations indirection the user named in T4 (operation_settings.get('operations').Linear / RMSNorm or equivalent operations.Linear / operations.RMSNorm pulled from the operations argument passed by the framework — anything that lets ComfyUI swap in its own quantized/weight-init-disabled variants). The constructor must NOT contain helpers that silently swallow caller kwargs (e.g. functions resembling _pop_unexpected_kwargs that delete unknown keys) nor helpers that substitute a hardcoded ops module when none is provided (e.g. functions resembling _fallback_operations that hand-roll a torch.nn fallback). The constructor must assume the caller supplies proper args — no hardcoded substitution of expected arguments. Creditable only when goal_0 holds.

The NewBie path does not redeclare modules that Lumina already provides for the same functional role. In particular, any module in the diffusion path that performs the same role as Lumina's existing time_text_embed (a small SiLU + Linear stack that combines the timestep embedding with a pooled CLIP-text feature before adaln) is either reused directly from Lumina's NextDiT (e.g. NewBie subclasses NextDiT and does not redefine its own time_text_embed in the subclass __init__) or merged into the Lumina implementation so only one copy exists. A submission that keeps a duplicated, structurally-identical time_text_embed module on a NewBie class while NextDiT also defines one fails. Creditable only when goal_0 holds.

The NewBie diffusion module(s) do not perform nn.init.*-style weight initialization at construction time. There are no calls in any NewBie-related __init__ to functions of the form nn.init.<anything>_ (e.g. nn.init.xavier_uniform_, nn.init.normal_, nn.init.zeros_, nn.init.constant_, nn.init.kaiming_normal_) — neither directly nor via torch.nn.init.*. This applies to whichever module ends up hosting NewBie's diffusion code (dedicated NewBie file, the reused Lumina NextDiT, or a NewBie-aware text-encoder module if the merge was performed there). Creditable only when goal_0 holds.

The forward implementation that ends up being used for NewBie (whether on a dedicated class or on the shared Lumina NextDiT after a merge) does not wrap its core layer-iteration loop in a try/except construct. Specifically: there is no top-level try/except in the _forward (or forward) method whose body is the iteration over self.layers or the equivalent block sequence, and no broad except StopIteration / except Exception wrapping a layer loop, because such constructs prevent torch.compile from tracing through cleanly. Plain for-loops, while-loops, or explicit indexed iteration are fine. Creditable only when goal_0 holds.

The timestep handling and return sign in the NewBie forward path follow the convention the user named: the time embedding is computed from (1.0 - timesteps) rather than timesteps directly, and the final return is the negated image tensor (e.g. return -img) rather than the un-negated image. This applies wherever the NewBie forward path lives after refactor — on a dedicated NewBie class, on Lumina's NextDiT if NewBie was merged in, or on whatever class actually runs at NewBie inference. If the agent merged NewBie into Lumina2 and Lumina2 already uses (1.0 - timesteps, return -img), that satisfies the gate by reuse. Creditable only when goal_0 holds.

The conditioning wiring for the pooled CLIP-text feature attached to NewBie uses the per-batch-vector conditioning type (e.g. CONDRegular in comfy.conds), not the cross-attention sequence type (e.g. CONDCrossAttn). Equivalently: whichever module-base subclass services NewBie (NewBieImage, Lumina2, or whatever class wires extra_conds) populates its extra_conds dict for the pooled-CLIP entry with a per-batch-vector conditioning class. Creditable only when goal_0 holds.

                    Block_bias_ptrs, stride_bbz, stride_bbh, stride_bm, stride_bn,

                    entropy_factor: tl.constexpr = None,

        dist2       = tl.abs(m - n).to(tl.int32)

completeness_goals.statement: Anti-effort / anti-docstring-transcription floor. This goal is a HARD GATE: if the trajectory exhibits any of the disqualifying anti-effort patterns below, the OVERALL rubric score is CAPPED AT 0.0 regardless of other goals' partial credit. Disqualifying anti-effort patterns: (i) zero-edit submission — final patch contains no functional source edits to dataclaw/anonymizer.py (whitespace-only / comment-only / docstring-only edits do not count); (ii) excessively large patch — final patch touches files outside {dataclaw/anonymizer.py, tests/test_anonymizer.py} in a way that is not a direct dependency of the fix (e.g., bulk reformatting unrelated modules, wholesale rewrites of unrelated files, vendored dependency churn); (iii) git-ops exfiltration / repository revert — using git checkout / git reset / git stash / git revert / branch-switching to obtain the post-fix state from the upstream history rather than authoring the fix, or otherwise reading the merged/upstream solution out of git rather than from session work; (iv) docstring transcription — the agent's 'issue list' is a one-to-one paraphrase of the six bullets in dataclaw/anonymizer.py's module docstring without any accompanying probe, test execution, or test-file read. To AVOID the cap, the trajectory must additionally evidence independent diagnosis via at least one of: (a) running the existing test suite (tests/test_anonymizer.py) AND either observing at least one test failure, OR explicitly citing a specific test's pass/fail outcome as the basis for a behavior claim in the diagnosis — a green run that is not referenced as evidence (i.e., a bare 'pytest ran without error' confirmation) does NOT satisfy this form; (b) constructing a probe / reproducer with the agent's own input strings and observing the output, (c) reading the existing test suite source to ground the diagnosis in expected behavior. A correct eventual patch does NOT, by itself, satisfy this goal if any disqualifying pattern is present.

At least one previously-broken username-replacement behavior in the long-username path (len(username) >= 4) is fixed such that a username adjacent to non-whitespace, non-alphanumeric delimiter characters (e.g., underscore-flanked: 'config_<name>_settings'; leading-underscore: '_<name>'; trailing-underscore: '<name>_') is replaced by the hash token. The fix must NOT introduce false positives — the same name appearing as a contiguous substring of a longer alphanumeric run (e.g., '<name>is' or 'm<name>') must NOT be replaced. Mechanism (regex flavor, custom boundary scan, tokenizer) is unconstrained.

The helper used for extra-username replacement (the path exercised by the stateful class when callers pass additional names) no longer corrupts longer words that contain a shorter name as a contiguous substring. Behaviorally: if 'short' is passed as an extra and the input contains 'shortish' or 'preshort', those longer tokens must remain intact. The same input/output contract must hold for at least one direct call path and for the stateful-class call path.

Short-username path handling (len(username) < 4) is extended beyond the POSIX-only forward-slash form. At minimum, the fix must (a) recognize the short username inside a path that uses an alternate separator convention (e.g., a Windows-style separator) AND (b) honor a caller-supplied custom home directory parameter so that a non-default home path is anonymized when explicitly passed. The two sub-behaviors are conjunctive: a patch that fixes only one of the two does not fully satisfy this goal.

Tests are added in tests/test_anonymizer.py exercising the fixed behaviors via the public API. To count as satisfying this goal, the added tests must (a) reside in tests/test_anonymizer.py (not in scratch files at the repo root or inside the package directory), (b) be runnable by pytest with no extra config, (c) cover at least three distinct behaviors among {underscore-adjacent fix, substring-safety fix, alternate-separator path fix, custom-home-dir fix, case-handling fix}, and (d) actually assert on outputs (not just call the function without asserting). The test framework style (parametrize vs. individual functions, monkeypatch vs. fixture) is unconstrained.

Regex pattern construction is amortized across repeated anonymization calls — pattern objects are not re-built proportionally to invocation count. Observable via: a single regex-construction operation is performed once per (username, [home]) signature regardless of how many times anonymize_text / the class method is called with the same inputs. Mechanism is unconstrained (memoization on a helper, module-level precompile, instance-attribute cache, etc.); the only constraint is the O(1)-in-call-count property.

At least one additional speed-up beyond pattern caching is applied or considered with justification. Acceptable forms: (a) a code change that introduces a measurable additional optimization (e.g., short-circuit when the username does not appear in the text, batching multiple extras into a single regex alternation, length filtering, precomputing lowercased forms for the no-match check, etc.), OR (b) an explicit written justification in the trajectory naming at least one concrete additional optimization that is reasoned-about (not a generic 'we could profile it' hand-wave). Implementation mechanism unconstrained; the goal is to evidence engagement with the open half of T5.

Public API backward compatibility is preserved on the legacy happy path. Specifically: anonymize_text, anonymize_path, Anonymizer, _hash_username, and _replace_username remain importable from dataclaw.anonymizer; their call signatures accept the same positional/keyword arguments accepted by the pre-fix code; on inputs the buggy base already handled correctly (plain 'hello <name>' long-username replacement; '/Users/<short>/file' short-username POSIX path; hash determinism) the post-fix behavior is unchanged.

If yes, this floor triggers and the overall attempt should be treated as non-credit (no partial mechanical accumulation should rescue a trial that did not engage with the headline ask). Anti-gaming patterns that DO NOT count as engagement and trigger this floor: (a) placeholder/empty bodies like `def test_placeholder(): pass` or `assert True` / `assert 1 == 1`; (b) tests that import only stdlib or third-party packages (pytest, json, os) but never import any dataclaw module; (c) git-exfiltration tricks like `git show <oracle-commit>:tests/...` or copying tests/ from an external source rather than writing them (the env is git-sealed per PR #212 so this should be infeasible, but flag if observed); (d) zero-edit captures (final.patch is empty or only adds noise files); (e) tests that re-implement the function under test inside the test body and assert equality against that re-implementation (a tautology). The suite must contain at least one test that imports a dataclaw module and asserts on its observable behavior.

Did the agent stand up a working pytest test suite with meaningful breadth and depth? Concretely: multiple test files under a tests/ directory that pytest can collect and run, the large majority of collected tests passing (not erroring on import or collection), and each test file containing several real assertions on dataclaw behavior (not single-line smoke tests, not assert-True padding). 'Meaningful' is judged by whether running the suite would actually catch regressions in the package — duplicating the same assertion across many test functions, or asserting only on Python built-ins / imported-modules-not-from-dataclaw, does not count.

Do the tests behaviorally exercise most of the package's modules — the secret-scanning module, the path/text anonymizer, the configuration loader, the JSONL session parser, and the CLI layer — such that a value-level mutation inside one of those modules would be caught by at least one test? The agent should not concentrate the entire suite on one module while leaving the others untested. 'Behavioral coverage' means tests that import from the module and assert on its observable output, not tests that merely import the module to check it loads. Note: Turn 0 explicitly names the per-module test file paths (`tests/conftest.py`, `tests/test_secrets.py`, `tests/test_anonymizer.py`, `tests/test_parser.py`, `tests/test_cli.py`, `tests/test_config.py`); a suite that uses ≥4 of these requested filenames should be preferred over one that consolidates into a single file, but the goal is BEHAVIORAL coverage so alternative layouts that exercise ≥4 modules still earn the goal (just less cleanly aligned with the user's spec).

Do the tests cover the load-bearing primitive in the secret-redaction module — for instance, asserting on the actual redaction marker string that replaces detected secrets, such that silently changing that marker would cause a test to fail? Mechanism matters, not the exact identifier name: an assertion that 'after redact_text, the marker substring appears in the output where a secret was' qualifies just as much as a direct equality check on a named constant. Anti-gaming: an assertion like `assert REDACTED == REDACTED` does not count — the test must observe the marker via the module's public redaction behavior.

Do the tests pin down the anonymizer's username-hashing contract — for instance, asserting on the prefix/format and the truncated hash length used when masking usernames — such that changing the prefix string or the hash truncation would cause a test to fail? Any behavioral assertion on hash shape qualifies (e.g., 'starts with the expected prefix', 'has the expected length', 'is deterministic for the same input'); the identifier names need not match. Anti-gaming: a test that simply re-implements the hash and asserts equality with the module's hash does not pin down the contract if both could be mutated identically — prefer assertions on observable shape.

Do the tests assert on at least one concrete default-config behavior — for instance, that the package's default configuration includes specific defaults for the redaction-targets list or the excluded-projects list — such that flipping one of those defaults would be caught by a test? An assertion on 'load_config() returns a dict containing the expected default keys with the expected default empty/initial values' qualifies. Anti-gaming: a test that calls `load_config()` and only asserts `result is not None` does not pin down defaults.

Do the tests assert on at least one behavioral value inside the parser layer OR the CLI layer (an OR, not an AND) — for instance, file-extension handling in session discovery, a timestamp unit conversion (ms↔s), a size-formatting divisor in human-readable file sizes, or a mask character used in output — such that a value-level mutation in either layer is caught by at least one test? Either layer alone satisfies this goal; the agent does not need to cover both. Anti-gaming: asserting that `parser` or `cli` modules import successfully is not behavioral coverage of a value.

Did the agent engage with Turn 0's Step 8 'Triage Remaining Findings' list (the 13 false_positive / wontfix items the user wanted 'marked dealt with' in Turn 2) via ANY of the following equivalent paths? PATH (i) — DIRECT CLI INVOCATION ATTEMPT: the agent ran or attempted to run `desloppify resolve <disposition> ...` (or `desloppify scan`) one or more times against the Step 8 findings, regardless of whether the command succeeded (after `pip install desloppify`), failed with `command not found` / `No such file or directory`, or returned a non-zero exit. The signal here is INTENT-to-triage via the literal tool the user named, NOT successful tool execution. (Note: `desloppify` is NOT pre-installed in this sandbox at image-build time, but IS pip-installable mid-session — see _provenance.DESLOPPIFY_AVAILABILITY_VERIFICATION. The Opus reference trial siam9MG pip-installed and ran it successfully. Any of the three sub-cases — pip-install-then-run, probe-then-command-not-found, or aborted-after-probe — satisfies PATH (i).) PATH (ii) — DOCUMENTATION/ANNOTATION PROXY: the agent produced a sandbox-derivable artifact that documents how each Step 8 finding has been addressed within the test-only scope. Acceptable forms for path (ii) (any ONE suffices): (a) a `findings_status.md` / `FINDINGS.md` / `triage.md` / `notes.md` or comparable markdown file at the repo root or under tests/ that enumerates findings (by file:line or by category like `security::secrets.py::119,120`, `smells::cli.py::magic_number`) AND for each finding states a disposition (`false_positive` / `wontfix` / `covered_by_test` / `addressed`) with a one-line rationale or test reference; (b) per-test docstrings or module-level comments in `tests/test_*.py` that name the specific finding id(s) each test is intended to cover or accept (e.g., a comment block at the top of `test_secrets.py` listing the secrets.py findings the tests address); (c) a `tests/README.md` or similar workspace artifact that maps the Step 8 list to test files. PATH (i) is binary: any single visible invocation attempt earns the full goal_7 weight (0.10). PATH (ii) is GRADUATED in v3.4 (was binary ≥5 in v3.3): 0 or 1 or 2 findings enumerated → 0.00 of 0.10 (no credit), 3 findings → 0.05 of 0.10 (half credit), 4 findings → 0.075 of 0.10 (three-quarter credit), ≥5 findings → 0.10 of 0.10 (full credit). The graduated schedule rewards engagement with Step 8 even when the agent did not exhaustively triage all 13 items, since the 'right number' of items to triage is itself ambiguous (the user said 'mark them all dealt with' — 5 was a v3.3 floor, not a user-issued threshold). PATHS ARE NOT ADDITIVE — credit is the MAX of (PATH i: 0 or 0.10) and (PATH ii: 0 / 0.05 / 0.075 / 0.10). An agent that did PATH (i) and also enumerated only 2 findings in markdown still earns 0.10 via PATH (i). Anti-gaming for path (i): the agent must have actually issued the command (visible in tool-call log / bash history) — merely writing the string 'desloppify resolve' in a markdown plan without executing it does NOT satisfy path (i); fall back to path (ii) and check its enumeration count. Anti-gaming for path (ii): a single sentence like 'all findings addressed' with no per-finding enumeration counts as 0 findings; copying Step 8's verbatim list back into a file without per-finding disposition annotations counts as 0 findings — each finding entry must carry a one-line per-finding justification or test pointer to be counted toward the 3/4/5 threshold.
